nodes.label: Functions
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A function f: A → B maps each element of domain A to exactly one element of codomain B. Key concepts: domain, codomain, range, injectivity (one-to-one), surjectivity (onto), bijectivity. Function composition f∘g means apply g first then f. Inverse functions f⁻¹ reverse the mapping when f is bijective.

nodes.label: Limits
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The limit lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a (not necessarily at x=a). Limits can exist even when f(a) is undefined. One-sided limits (left and right) must agree for the limit to exist. L'Hôpital's rule applies when limits give 0/0 or ∞/∞ form. Limits are the rigorous foundation of all of calculus.

nodes.label: Continuity
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A function is continuous at x=a if: f(a) is defined, lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a). Discontinuities: removable (hole), jump, infinite. The intermediate value theorem states a continuous function on [a,b] takes all values between f(a) and f(b). Differentiability implies continuity — but not vice versa.

nodes.label: Derivatives
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The derivative f'(x) = lim_{h→0} (f(x+h)−f(x))/h is the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the tangent line at a point. Geometrically: the slope of the tangent line. Physically: instantaneous velocity. The derivative of x² is 2x (power rule). The derivative of sin(x) is cos(x). A function is differentiable at a point if the derivative exists there.

nodes.label: Differentiation Rules
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Key rules: Power rule d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. Product rule (fg)' = f'g+fg'. Quotient rule (f/g)' = (f'g−fg')/g². Chain rule (f∘g)' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Derivatives of standard functions: sin→cos, cos→−sin, eˣ→eˣ, ln(x)→1/x. The chain rule is the most commonly misapplied rule.

nodes.label: Higher Derivatives
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The second derivative f''(x) measures how the rate of change is itself changing — concavity. f'' > 0: concave up (holds water). f'' < 0: concave down (spills water). An inflection point is where concavity changes. The second derivative test for optimization: if f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0 then c is a local minimum; f''(c)<0 means local maximum.

nodes.label: Mean Value Theorem
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c in (a,b) with f'(c) = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a). Geometrically: there is a point where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line. Rolle's theorem is the special case f(a)=f(b). MVT has profound implications for bounding function values.
aliases: average rate of change equals instantaneous

nodes.label: Optimization
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Finding extrema: set f'(x)=0 to find critical points. First derivative test: sign change of f' at c. Second derivative test: sign of f''(c). Global extrema on [a,b]: check critical points and endpoints. Optimization problems model real-world maxima/minima (maximize area, minimize cost). Lagrange multipliers handle constrained optimization.

nodes.label: Related Rates
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Related rates problems use implicit differentiation with respect to time. If two quantities are related by an equation, differentiating both sides with respect to t gives a relationship between their rates of change. Key: identify all variables, write the relationship equation, differentiate both sides with respect to t using chain rule.

nodes.label: Integration
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is the signed area under the curve f(x) from a to b. It is defined as the limit of Riemann sums. The indefinite integral (antiderivative) ∫f(x)dx = F(x)+C where F'(x)=f(x). Integration is more complex than differentiation — not all functions have elementary antiderivatives.

nodes.label: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The FTC has two parts: (1) If F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt then F'(x) = f(x) — differentiation and integration are inverse operations. (2) ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f. This connects the two main operations of calculus and allows definite integrals to be computed without Riemann sums.

nodes.label: Integration Techniques
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Key techniques: U-substitution (reverse chain rule): ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx. Integration by parts: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Trigonometric substitution. Partial fractions for rational functions. These techniques reduce complex integrals to known forms. Choosing the right technique is an art that comes with practice.

nodes.label: Sequences and Series
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A sequence {aₙ} converges if lim_{n→∞} aₙ exists. A series Σaₙ converges if the sequence of partial sums converges. Key convergence tests: ratio test, comparison test, integral test, alternating series test. A geometric series Σarⁿ converges to a/(1−r) for |r|<1. Absolute convergence implies convergence.

nodes.label: Taylor Series
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A Taylor series represents a function as an infinite sum of terms involving its derivatives at a point: f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! · (x−a)ⁿ. Maclaurin series: expansion about a=0. Key series: eˣ = 1+x+x²/2!+..., sin(x) = x−x³/3!+..., cos(x) = 1−x²/2!+.... Taylor polynomials approximate functions locally. Radius of convergence determines where the series is valid.

nodes.label: Differential Equations
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: An ODE involves a function and its derivatives: dy/dx = f(x,y). Separable ODEs: separate variables and integrate both sides. First-order linear ODEs: integrating factor method. Second-order linear ODEs (constant coefficients) have characteristic equations. Applications: population growth, cooling, oscillators. Initial conditions determine the specific solution.

nodes.label: Multivariable Calculus
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Extension of calculus to functions of multiple variables f(x,y,z). Partial derivatives: ∂f/∂x treats other variables as constants. The gradient ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂f/∂z) points in the direction of steepest ascent. Double and triple integrals. The Jacobian measures volume distortion under change of variables.

nodes.label: Vector Calculus
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Vector calculus extends calculus to vector fields. Divergence ∇·F measures sources/sinks of a field. Curl ∇×F measures rotation of a field. Line integrals ∫_C F·dr compute work done by a field along a curve. Surface integrals. Fundamental theorems: Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, Divergence theorem — all generalize the FTC to higher dimensions.

nodes.label: Epsilon-Delta Definition
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The rigorous ε-δ definition of limit: lim_{x→a} f(x)=L means for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that 0<|x−a|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε. This makes precise what 'arbitrarily close' means. Similarly, continuity at a: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |x−a|<δ implies |f(x)−f(a)|<ε.
aliases: for all epsilon there exists delta

nodes.label: Riemann Integral
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The Riemann integral formalizes the area under a curve as a limit of Riemann sums: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = lim_{n→∞} Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx. Left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums are approximations. A function is Riemann integrable on [a,b] if it is bounded and continuous almost everywhere. Upper and lower sums bound the integral.

nodes.label: Implicit Differentiation
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Implicit differentiation differentiates both sides of an equation with respect to x when y is implicitly defined (not solved for explicitly). Apply chain rule whenever differentiating y: d/dx(y²) = 2y·dy/dx. Used for curves like circles x²+y²=r² where solving for y requires two branches.

nodes.label: L'Hôpital's Rule
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: L'Hôpital's rule: if lim f(x)/g(x) gives 0/0 or ∞/∞ form, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f'(x)/g'(x), provided the latter limit exists. It can be applied repeatedly. Other indeterminate forms (0·∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰) can be converted to 0/0 or ∞/∞ form first.

nodes.label: Area and Volume by Integration
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Area between curves: ∫[f(x)−g(x)]dx. Volume of revolution by disk method: π∫[f(x)]²dx. Shell method: 2π∫x·f(x)dx. Arc length: ∫√(1+(f'(x))²)dx. Surface area of revolution: 2π∫f(x)√(1+(f'(x))²)dx. These applications connect definite integration to geometric measurement.
